To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the loss of significance in floating point addition and subtraction is: (a) a function of the number of βits in the significand, (b) a function of β, (c) a function of whether the operands are selected from the logarithmic or the uniform distribution, and (d) a function of how many bits are shifted.

for addition, the probability of losing a significant βit is about (1.5/β) × 2-k, for subtraction it is about (1/β) × (1.5)k, and for addition/subtraction, the probability of a loss of more than m βits is about (1/(β-1)) × (1.2)m.

(1) the probability of a shift of m βit(s) is approximately equal to the binomial probability of a shift by m bits in the corresponding base 2 case (i.e., the probability of a 2-bit shift is about 0.25, the probability of a four-bit shift is about (0.25)4, and so on); and (2) the probability of the shift is independent of the base β.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the loss of significance is more likely for addition than subtraction, and more likely for the uniform distribution than the logarithmic distribution.
the loss of significant bits is a random process.
the probability of a normalization shift is approximately 1/β for the uniform distribution, and 2/β for the logarithmic distribution.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, if the operands are selected from the uniform distribution, then the probability of an m-bit shift, for m = 1, 2,..., β, is given by the following formula, which holds for all bases: Pr{m-bit shift | exponent difference of k bits} = 1 β ( β−k β ) β−m β.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the loss of significance is much higher for addition/subtraction than it is for multiplication/division.
the loss of significance is much more severe for floating point subtraction than for floating point addition.
the loss of significance in floating point arithmetic can be predicted by the difference in exponents of the two operands.
